phonemes.desc: Open syllable with short [a], from the Akkadian root lahāmu, 'to be hairy'.
Voiceless velar fricative [x], written with the cuneiform ḫu sign — the consonant that separates Lahmu from a simple English h.
Bilabial nasal [m] plus close back vowel [u], the masculine nominative ending.

pronunciation.approximation: 'LAKH-moo' — the middle consonant is a dry, breathy 'kh' like the ch in Scottish 'loch', not a soft English h.

pronunciation.note: Lahmu is Tier 2 because the registrable canonical form is plain ASCII: it preserves no distinctive diacritic or non-Latin letter. Scholarly Assyriological transliteration often writes Laḫmu with an underdot ḫ to mark the voiceless velar fricative, but the PuniCodex flagship temple displays the unadorned Latin form Lahmu.

domains.title: LAHMU — The Hairy Guardian
domains.subtitle: Primordial Protector · Gatekeeper · Silt and Threshold
domains.lead:
Lahmu is the Mesopotamian primordial being whose name simply means 'the hairy one'. In the Enuma Elish he is the firstborn of Apsû and Tiāmat, the earliest divine generation before sky and earth were fixed. Beyond cosmogony, he is a protective spirit: a bearded, hair-covered guardian posted at doorways, gates, and thresholds to turn aside demons and pollution.

He stands at the border between chaos and order — born from the mingled primordial waters, then stationed at the doors that keep the ordered world safe.

cards.name: Primordial Firstborn
cards.desc: First child of Apsû and Tiāmat; the divine line that leads to Anshar, Kishar, Anu, and Ea begins with him.

cards.name: Guardian of the Gate
cards.desc: In ritual and iconography Lahmu protects temple and palace doorways, the hairy sentinel at the threshold.

cards.name: The Hairy One
cards.desc: His name and form declare the power of hair: the beard, the mane, the shaggy pelt that marks the apotropaic demon.

cards.name: Paired with Lahamu
cards.desc: Lahmu and Lahamu appear together as a twin protective pair, male and female guardians of the entrance.

mythology.lead: Lahmu is not a protagonist of long narrative cycles; his power is concentrated at origins and thresholds. He appears at the very beginning of the Babylonian cosmos, and he endures at the edges of the ordered world as a guardian.

myths.title: Firstborn of the Primordial Waters
myths.text: The Enuma Elish opens with Apsû, the freshwater abyss, and Tiāmat, the salt sea. Their waters mingled and produced the first generation of gods: Lahmu and Lahamu, then Anshar and Kishar, then Anu, and finally Ea (Enuma Elish I:1–10). Lahmu is therefore the first divine body to emerge from chaos, the earliest shape the cosmos takes after the waters meet.

myths.title: The Hairy Doorkeeper
myths.text: In ritual texts and iconography Lahmu is a protective demon stationed at doorways. His shaggy body and beard were believed to frighten away evil. Clay figurines and glazed reliefs show him as a muscular, bearded male with curled hair, often flanking an entrance. To pass his gate was to move from dangerous outside into protected inside.

myths.title: The Six-Curled Guardian
myths.text: Lahmu is recognizable in Mesopotamian art by his long beard arranged in six or seven rounded curls, a naked or lightly clad hairy body, and an aggressive stance. He sometimes grasps a weapon or a gatepost. These attributes made him instantly readable as an apotropaic figure: the hair that named him became the visual sign of his power.

myths.title: Lahmu and Lahamu
myths.text: Lahmu is paired with Lahamu, a feminine counterpart whose name shares the same root. Together they guard entrances and thresholds, male and female aspects of a single protective function. In the Enuma Elish the pair is born together; in ritual art they are often depicted as matching figures on either side of a door.

syncretism:
Lahmu's double life — primordial ancestor and doorway demon — gave him a long afterlife in Mesopotamian religion.

As a cosmogonic figure he belongs to the same watery genealogy as Apsû and Tiāmat, and through them his memory survives in biblical and Near Eastern images of the primordial deep. As a guardian he anticipates the apotropaic figures of later traditions: the cherubim posted at Eden's east gate, the lion and bull colossi that guard Assyrian palace doors, and the sphinxes and lamassu that still flank temple entrances across the ancient Near East. The Greek daimon and the Roman genius loci partly overlap with his function, though none carry his distinctive hairy form.
culturalLegacy:
The hairy guardian never fully left the architectural imagination.

Every bearded gatekeeper figure, from Assyrian palace reliefs to medieval church gargoyles and the lion-headed knockers of later doors, preserves the old idea that a threshold needs a frightening friend. In cuneiform studies the name Lahmu remains a standard example of how a descriptive adjective — 'the hairy one' — could become a deity. Modern fantasy and games often borrow Mesopotamian 'hairy demons' without knowing their source, but the type is authentically ancient. PuniCodex keeps the plain Latin form Lahmu as a Tier-2 node: a reminder that not every restoration needs a diacritic; some names are powerful precisely because they are plain.
archaeology: Archaeological evidence for Lahmu consists chiefly of protective figurines, glazed brick reliefs, and seal impressions. Neo-Assyrian palace gateways, notably at Khorsabad and Nineveh, were flanked by apotropaic colossi whose iconography overlaps with the lahmu type. Clay figurines buried in foundation deposits and door sockets invoke his protective function. Cuneiform copies of the Enuma Elish from Nineveh and Babylon preserve his cosmogonic role.
